newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr levels out at dizzying heights.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr levels out at dizzying heights.

text.p: The Australian dollar stepped back a little Friday from the dizzying heights reached offshore but still looked well placed to extend its bull run.

Five months of frustration had ended in a wildly impulsive move Thursday as the currency cleared no less than five major resistance levels, absorbed massive amounts of selling and stopped dozens of banks out of huge options positions.

It rose 2-1/4 cents, hit six-year highs and caught the eye of chart watchers who saw 84 cents on the horizon. Some profit taking did emerge today, but the pullback was slight and dealers expected US$0.8050 to hold for a tilt at US$0.8150 next week.

By 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the local dollar had edged back to US$0.8085/90 after suffering a touch of vertigo at an offshore peak of US$0.8125. It was still up on Thursday's US$.8080/85 and a world away from its US$0.7904/09 close last week.

Traders said some U.S. funds which had been big buyers through the week booked a few profits today and there were signs of options-related selling following the flood of forced bids Thursday when months old ranges gave way.
This was parlty soaked up by buying for another yen/A$ dual currency samurai bond -- a 20 billion yen issue was launched for the Australian Wheat Board.
There was strong chart support at US$0.8050, which marked the former peak for the year, and analysts reckoned it would take a breach of US$0.7950 to turn the tide against the bulls.
Resistance had made an appearance at US$0.8120 but there was talk of hefty stop loss buy orders around US$0.8130 which could see the currency to at least US$0.8150 if triggered.

On the crosses the currency was holding at 90.10/20 yen having surged to 90.16/26 late Thursday from 88.65/64 the day before. It was up at 59.4 on its trade weighted index -- a five year high -- from 59.2.
Noteable gains were made on the Canadian and Kiwi dollars.

Traders said some well known New York funds had switched back to the A$ after flirting with these two for the last month or so. Against the Canadian dollar, for instance, it had soared to C$1.0827/37 from a trough of C$1.0369 just a fortnight ago.
Analysts noted that one interesting side effect of this strength was that it made another monetary easing by the Reserve Bank more likely.

"The rise in the dollar is a de-facto tightening of policy which it's hard to believe the RBA will welcome only a couple of weeks after it cut rates," said Craig James, senior economist at Colonial State Bank.
"It will also bear down on inflation, so another cut looks a little more likely," he said.
The money market agreed and pushed the March 90-day bank bill future up eight basis points to 93.88, implying a rate of 6.12 percent against the present official rate of 6.5 percent.
That risk could give dollar bulls some pause, although dealers noted that dollar yields would still be far above those in Japan even if official rates were cut.
And there seemed to be little risk of Japanese rates rising anytime soon given the fragility of the banking system there as evidenced by the failure of Hanwa Bank this week.

The dollar's supporters also pointed out that Canada had been cutting rates every month this year and its currency had still risen steadily reflecting improved prospects for the economy next year and a favourable inflation performance.
Australian inflation had also fallen markedly and was set to remain under that in the U.S. for a year or more, which should also work to keep A$ assets attractive even if short term rates fall.
